title: Alerting thresholds are an editorial choice
lead: A threshold looks like a technical setting. It is really a statement about what your organisation considers worth waking someone up for, and it should be argued about in those terms.
author: Licter analysis team
prose:
The number is the least interesting part

Set an alert at three hundred mentions an hour and you will be told about football. Set it at thirty and you will be told about everything. Teams spend weeks tuning that number and very little time on the question underneath it: what are we actually trying not to miss?

Two organisations with identical volumes can be right to set wildly different thresholds, because they are exposed to different things. A retailer fears a product safety claim spreading in a parenting community at low volume. A public body fears a mid-volume rumour with political pickup. Those are not the same alert.

Twenty mentions in a market where you normally see fifteen a week is the entire story.

Threshold per topic, per market

A single global threshold is a guarantee of two failures at once: noise in your largest market and silence in your smallest. Twenty mentions in a market where you normally see two hundred a day is nothing. Twenty mentions in a market where you normally see fifteen a week is the entire story.

Per-topic matters as much. Recruitment chatter and product failure chatter should not share a trigger, because the cost of missing them is not comparable.

Write down the cost of a miss

The clean way to settle threshold arguments is to make the trade explicit. For each topic, write one line: what happens if we hear about this six hours late. Some answers are “nothing”. Some are not. The thresholds fall out of the list almost by themselves, and — more usefully — the list is reviewable by people who do not read dashboards.

It also gives you something to point at when someone asks why they were paged at two in the morning.

What to take away

  • Thresholds encode what you are willing to miss.
  • One global threshold guarantees noise in big markets and silence in small ones.
  • Set them per topic and per market.
  • Write the cost of a six-hour delay for each topic, and let the numbers follow.

title: Behaviour against declaration
lead: The strongest consumer insight is usually the one where somebody’s stated preference and their observable behaviour come apart. Finding those gaps is a method, not luck.
author: Licter analysis team
prose:
Start from the contradiction, not the topic

Most insight briefs start from a subject: what do people think about our category. The output is a description, and descriptions rarely change decisions.

A more productive starting point is a contradiction you already suspect. Customers say price is the reason they leave; retention data says they leave after a service failure. Now the conversation data has a job: which of those two shows up when people talk unprompted, and in what proportion?

People talk to brands differently than they talk about them.

Where to look for the gap

Reviews and complaint threads are where declaration collapses, because the person is motivated and unobserved. Comparison and recommendation threads — someone asking a community what to buy — are where the real decision criteria surface, because the stakes are personal and the audience is peers.

Advertising and brand accounts are the worst place to look. The conversation there is with the brand, and people talk to brands differently than they talk about them.

The output that survives the meeting

A gap finding is only actionable if it names the decision it changes. “People say price, they discuss service” is interesting. “People say price, they discuss service, and the service complaints cluster in the two weeks after delivery” is a brief for an operations team.

Specificity about when and where is what turns an insight into a piece of work somebody can be assigned.

What to take away

  • Start from a suspected contradiction, not a topic.
  • Reviews and peer recommendation threads carry real criteria.
  • Brand-owned channels are the worst place to look for them.
  • Name the decision the gap changes, with a when and a where.

title: Language coverage is not translation
lead: A tool that reports twenty languages is telling you about collection, not about understanding. The gap between the two is where most multi-market reads go wrong.
author: Licter analysis team
prose:
Three different claims

“We collect in twenty languages” means the crawler does not choke on the character set. “We classify in twenty languages” means sentiment and topic models exist for each. “We understand twenty languages” means somebody who speaks them has looked at the output. Vendors are usually making the first claim in the vocabulary of the third.

The distinction is not pedantic. Collection without classification gives you volume charts you cannot read. Classification without review gives you confident charts that are wrong in ways you cannot see.

The chart will show those markets as quiet. They are not quiet; they are invisible.

Where it breaks

Irony and negation are the classic failures, and they are unevenly distributed across languages. So are brand names that are also common words, which turn one market’s perimeter into noise while the neighbouring market stays clean.

The subtler failure is category vocabulary. The words a market uses for a product benefit rarely map one to one, and a taxonomy built in the headquarters language will quietly under-count the markets that phrase things differently. The chart will show those markets as quiet. They are not quiet; they are invisible.

A cheap check

Take two hundred items per market, have a native speaker classify them by hand, and compare against the machine. It takes a day per market and it tells you exactly which markets you can report on and which ones need a caveat.

Nobody enjoys doing this. Every team that has done it has changed at least one conclusion.

What to take away

  • Collection, classification and understanding are three different claims.
  • Irony, negation and ambiguous brand names fail unevenly by language.
  • A taxonomy built in one language under-counts markets that phrase things differently.
  • Two hundred hand-coded items per market will tell you what you can report on.

title: The persona workshop, replaced
lead: Personas built in a room describe the people in the room. Built from observed affinities, they describe an audience, and they can be checked.
author: Licter analysis team
prose:
What the workshop actually produces

The classic persona exercise collects a team’s assumptions, formats them, and gives them a name and a stock photograph. The output feels like knowledge because it is written down, and it is very hard to argue with because there is nothing in it that can be wrong.

That is the real cost. Not that the personas are inaccurate, but that they are unfalsifiable, so they survive contact with every subsequent piece of evidence.

The problem is not that workshop personas are inaccurate. It is that they are unfalsifiable.

What observed segmentation changes

Building a segmentation from affinities, interests and overlaps means every segment has a size, a boundary and a set of things that are true of it. All three can be wrong, which means all three can be corrected.

It also produces segments nobody in the room would have proposed. The overlap between two audiences you assumed were distinct is a common one, and it is usually where the reach upside sits.

Keep the workshop, change its input

This is not an argument for deleting the workshop. The room is where the segmentation gets connected to product decisions, and that connection has to be made by people who own those decisions.

The change is what the room starts from. Walk in with observed segments and let the team argue about what to do with them, instead of walking in empty and letting the team invent the audience.

What to take away

  • Workshop personas encode the room’s assumptions and cannot be disproved.
  • Observed segments have a size, a boundary and checkable properties.
  • Unexpected overlaps are usually where reach upside sits.
  • Keep the workshop; change what it starts from.

title: The trend you already missed
lead: By the time a trend is legible enough to put in a deck, the decision it should have informed has usually been taken. That gap is organisational, not technical.
author: Licter analysis team
prose:
Detection is rarely the bottleneck

When a company discovers a shift late, the instinct is to blame the tool: the query was too narrow, the platform was not covered, the alert did not fire. Sometimes that is true. More often the signal was in the data for months and nobody was in a position to act on it.

The lag that matters is not between the conversation and the dashboard. It is between the dashboard and the meeting where budgets move.

The lag that matters is not between the conversation and the dashboard. It is between the dashboard and the meeting where budgets move.

Three places the time goes

Framing. A finding that does not map onto a decision somebody owns has nowhere to go. “Interest in refill formats is rising” is an observation. “Refill formats are being discussed by the same communities that drove our last packaging complaint” is the beginning of a decision.

Confidence. Teams sit on early reads because being early and wrong is punished more than being late and right. The fix is procedural: say out loud how confident you are and what would change your mind, so that being early stops being a bet on your reputation.

Calendar. Most insight functions report on a rhythm set by the reporting cycle, not by the conversation. A shift that becomes visible in week three waits until the monthly readout, then until the next steering committee. Two months gone, structurally.

What a shorter loop looks like

The teams that move fastest are not the ones with the best tools. They are the ones where the person reading the data can put an item on an agenda without a translation layer. That is an organisational design question, and it is usually answered by proximity: the analyst sits with the team that decides, or reports to someone who does.

Everything else — coverage, taxonomy, alerting — is downstream of that. A perfect perimeter reporting into a monthly slide deck will still be late.

What to take away

  • Late discovery is usually a routing problem, not a coverage problem.
  • Frame findings against a decision someone owns.
  • State confidence explicitly so early reads stop being career bets.
  • Reporting rhythm should follow the conversation, not the calendar.

title: The voices that actually carry
lead: Follower count measures how many people could see something. It says almost nothing about whether anything moves when they do.
author: Licter analysis team
prose:
Audience size is a ceiling, not a force

A large account tells you the maximum number of impressions available. Whether those impressions turn into conversation, and whether that conversation reaches anyone new, are separate questions that size does not answer.

The accounts that move a category are frequently mid-sized and specific. They sit inside a community rather than above it, and what they say gets repeated in the community’s own words.

They sit inside a community rather than above it, and what they say gets repeated in the community’s own words.

Three things worth measuring instead

Onward conversation. Not shares — shares are cheap. New threads started by other people, referencing the idea without linking the source.

Community reach beyond their own. Does the topic appear in communities where that account is not present? That is the difference between an audience and a bridge.

Vocabulary adoption. If the framing survives — if people start using the words that account introduced — something real happened. If the framing dies with the post, you bought impressions.

The uncomfortable consequence

Measured this way, some very expensive partnerships stop looking like partnerships and start looking like media buys. That is a legitimate thing to buy, but it should be bought under its own name and evaluated with media metrics.

The corollary is that the accounts that do carry are often not on anybody’s list, are not looking for a brief, and cost a fraction of the ones that are.

What to take away

  • Follower count is a ceiling on impressions, not evidence of movement.
  • Measure onward threads, not shares.
  • Reach into communities the account is not part of is the real signal.
  • If the framing dies with the post, you bought media — price it as media.

title: Weak signals, before they trend
lead: Most of what gets called a weak signal is just a small number. Here is the difference between a conversation that predicts a shift and one that only looks like it does.
author: Licter analysis team
prose:
The problem with small numbers

Every monitoring tool can show you a topic going from forty mentions to four hundred. That is a multiplication by ten, and it will be flagged as a spike by any threshold you set. It is also, almost always, nothing: a single account with reach, one article syndicated across a group, a hashtag borrowed by an unrelated community for a week.

A weak signal is not a small volume. It is a small volume that behaves in a particular way, and the behaviour is what you have to look for. Volume alone will hand you a list of accidents and call it foresight.

A weak signal is not a small volume. It is a small volume behaving in a particular way.

Three properties worth checking

It spreads across communities rather than inside one. A topic that triples inside a single community is a community being loud. A topic that appears in three communities that do not normally talk to each other, at low volume in each, is a topic finding structural purchase. The second one is much rarer and much more interesting.

It survives its first news cycle. Anything can peak. What matters is the floor afterwards. If the baseline after the peak is meaningfully above the baseline before it, something was retained. If it returns to exactly where it was, the conversation borrowed the topic and gave it back.

It changes vocabulary as it travels. A signal that matters gets reworded by each community that picks it up, because each one has to fit it to its own concerns. A signal that travels with identical phrasing everywhere is usually being distributed rather than adopted.

What this costs you in practice

Checking those three properties is not free. It means keeping a perimeter stable for long enough to have a real baseline, which rules out rebuilding your query every quarter. It means segmenting the conversation into communities before you measure it, not after. And it means accepting that most of what you look at will turn out to be noise, which is uncomfortable when someone is waiting for a finding.

The alternative is worse. A team that reports every spike burns its credibility inside two quarters, and by the time it sees something real nobody is listening.

What to do with one when you find it

Do not escalate it as a trend. Escalate it as a hypothesis with a date attached: here is what we think is forming, here is what we expect to see in six weeks if we are right, here is what would disprove it. Then go back and check.

That last step is the one that almost never happens, and it is the only one that makes the practice improve. A foresight function that never scores its own calls is producing opinions with charts.

What to take away

  • Spread across unconnected communities beats growth inside one.
  • Compare the floor after the peak to the floor before it.
  • Vocabulary that mutates as it travels is a sign of adoption, not distribution.
  • Escalate hypotheses with a review date, not trends.

title: What a platform cannot do on its own
lead: Listening suites are very good at three things and structurally bad at two others. Knowing which is which is most of what separates a useful setup from an expensive one.
author: Licter analysis team
prose:
What they do well

Collection at scale, deduplication, and retrieval. A modern suite will pull more sources, more reliably, and hold more history than anything you would build. That is genuinely hard engineering and it is worth paying for.

Classification against a taxonomy you defined. Once the categories are right, the machine applies them consistently, which is something a human panel does not do across ten thousand items.

Alerting on thresholds you set. Reliable, fast, and indifferent to whether it is Sunday.

Every query encodes a hypothesis about what counts. The software cannot make that call for you.

What they cannot do

Decide what the perimeter is. Every query encodes a hypothesis about what counts. Include the competitor and you are measuring a category; exclude them and you are measuring a brand. Neither is wrong, but the software cannot make that call, and a perimeter chosen by default is a perimeter chosen by someone who was not thinking about your question.

Tell you what the result means. Sentiment moved four points. That is a fact. Whether it is a crisis, a seasonal artefact, or a competitor’s campaign spilling into your feed is an interpretation, and interpretation is where the value is.

The setup that follows

If the platform is good at collection and classification and bad at framing and interpretation, the sensible arrangement is obvious: buy the platform, staff the framing, and never confuse a licence with a capability.

The failure mode we see most often is the reverse. An organisation buys seats, hands them to a team with no time to define the perimeter, and receives a dashboard nobody opens. The tool was never the problem.

What to take away

  • Platforms are strong on collection, classification and alerting.
  • They cannot choose your perimeter or interpret a move.
  • A perimeter chosen by default was chosen by someone not thinking about your question.
  • Buy the licence, staff the framing.

title: Where panels and surveys disagree
lead: When observed behaviour and declared intention point in opposite directions, the useful move is not to pick a winner. It is to work out which question each one actually answered.
author: Licter analysis team
prose:
They are not measuring the same thing

A survey asks what someone will do, in a context where they know they are being asked. Social data records what they said unprompted, to an audience they chose, for reasons that have nothing to do with your study. Neither is the truth; they are two different instruments pointed at two different moments.

Disagreement between them is therefore not a failure. It is information about the gap between how people present a decision and how they discuss it.

Disagreement is not a failure. It is information about the gap between how people present a decision and how they discuss it.

The usual shapes of disagreement

Declared higher than observed. Typical of anything with a social desirability attached — sustainability, health, thrift. People mean it when they say it and do not do it.

Observed higher than declared. Typical of anything slightly embarrassing, or simply too mundane to mention in a survey. Categories people use constantly and never think about.

Different segments entirely. The most interesting case: both instruments are right, about different people. The survey sample and the conversation population do not overlap as much as either side assumes.

Reconcile before you report

The reconciliation is worth doing explicitly and worth showing. Put the two numbers side by side, name the gap, and say what you think produces it. That single slide does more for the credibility of an insights function than any individual finding.

The alternative — quietly dropping whichever instrument disagreed with the recommendation — is how insight teams lose the room, usually about eighteen months later.

What to take away

  • Surveys measure prompted intention; social data records unprompted behaviour.
  • Social desirability inflates declaration; mundanity deflates it.
  • Sometimes both are right about different populations.
  • Show the reconciliation instead of dropping the inconvenient instrument.
